Peak Retail Inc. - Q2 Earnings Call Transcript

Operator:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Peak Retail Inc. Q2 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please also note, today's event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
Thank you, Operator. Good morning, and thank you for joining us today to discuss Peak Retail Inc.'s results for the second quarter. Joining me on today’s call are Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements, which are subject to risks and uncertainties. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

With that, I’ll turn the call over to Mike.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you, Sarah. Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I’m pleased to report Peak Retail Inc.'s performance for the second quarter. We continued to execute on our strategic priorities and delivered solid results despite the challenging macroeconomic environment.

Today I will cover four key aspects of our performance:

1. Overall Performance: We achieved exceptional labor costs and store payroll leverage, with payroll as a percentage of sales improving 90 basis points to 11.2% amid 7.2% comp store sales growth, thanks to higher sales per labor hour and tech-driven scheduling.

2. E-Commerce Growth: Our omnichannel initiatives, including BOPIS and curbside pickup, surged with omnichannel sales up 28% year-over-year to represent 42% of e-commerce GMV, driving margin expansion through efficient store fulfillment.

3. Store Performance: Inventory levels declined 14.2% year-over-year to $1.18 billion, accelerating turns to 5.1x and supporting gross margin gains by minimizing markdowns across categories like apparel and home goods.

4. Marketing Initiatives: We're affirming full-year guidance based on key assumptions like 2% to 4% comps, resilient consumer spending in essentials, and operational leverage, positioning us for margin expansion and EPS of $8.50 to $9.20.

We are confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value for our shareholders.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Lisa to provide more details on our financial results.

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thank you, Mike. Good morning. I'll provide a more detailed review of our financial performance for the second quarter.

Our total revenue for the quarter was $7.1 billion, an 8.4% increase compared to the same period last year. Gross margin was 38.4%, expanding 210 basis points primarily driven by inventory discipline, freight savings, shrinkage reductions, and promotional discipline. Operating expenses were $1.48 billion, representing 20.8% of revenue, reflecting strong SG&A leverage including occupancy efficiencies and labor optimization. Net income was $550 million, or $2.10 per share. We generated $850 million in cash flow from operations. Inventory levels are currently down 14.2% year-over-year at $1.18 billion, with turns improving meaningfully.

Let me dive deeper into some of these standout areas, starting with our labor costs and store payroll leverage, which has been a key driver of our margin expansion this quarter. In our brick-and-mortar retail operations spanning over 1,200 stores nationwide focused on apparel, home goods, and seasonal merchandise, labor is our largest controllable SG&A expense, typically around 10-12% of sales. Effective payroll leverage comes from boosting sales per labor hour, or SPLH, while fine-tuning store scheduling to align with demand fluctuations, and we're thrilled with the outcomes.

Store payroll costs came in at $285 million in Q2, rising only 1.8% year-over-year despite the 7.2% comp store sales increase and overall 8.4% top-line growth. This drove labor as a percentage of sales down 90 basis points to 11.2%, from 12.1% last year. Stacking two years, that's a 140 basis point gain from the 12.6% seen in the disrupted Q2 2022. Our SPLH jumped 5.3% to $142 per labor hour, surpassing the 4.1% industry average from the National Retail Federation's labor productivity index.

Robust traffic up 6.8% comp and higher conversions in core categories powered this, especially our Peak Everyday Essentials private label, which grew 12% on comps with elevated average transaction values. We flexed payroll smartly, keeping store hours per week at 68 versus 70 last year and growing total payroll hours just 0.9% to 4.2 million chain-wide.

Our tech investments are delivering big. Kronos Workforce Dimensions is now in 95% of stores, linked to Blue Yonder's AI forecasting, slashing scheduling errors 28% and overstaffing 15% during quieter periods like midweek mornings in urban prototypes. Self-checkout kiosks with NCR computer vision in 150 high-volume locations cut cashier hours 8-10% while NPS stayed at 92%. This echoes Target's SPLH progress, but our ROI is 3.5x in year one.

By region, Sunbelt performance shone with 110 basis points of leverage from 9.2% comps in Texas, Florida, and the Carolinas, aided by new stores, hurricane recovery demand, and lower wages at $16.80/hour versus the national $18.20. Northeast delivered 60 basis points despite 7% wage hikes via Peak Flex part-timers at 62% of hours. California was toughest at 12.8% of sales due to regulations and $20+ wages, but SPLH grew 4.1% through BOPIS where associates handle 25% more pickups per shift.

Wage inflation hit 4.2% industry-wide per NRF with 3.8% unemployment, our average hourly up 4.5% to $18.20 but offset by SPLH-linked incentives lifting retention to 78% above the 72% peer average. Peak Academy training in 1,000 stores enables quick role switches, upping productivity 6%.

For the future, $45 million in capex goes to 400 more self-checkouts and RFID to cut out-of-stocks 20%, freeing labor for customers. Omnichannel store fulfillment at 35% of e-comm yields $250+ SPLH versus $120 in-store. Q3 labor seen at 11.0-11.3% of sales on 4-6% comps, full-year 80-100 basis points leverage, better than Walmart's deleverage or Macy's urban issues. This discipline added $28 million to EBITDA—managing costs while fueling growth.

Shifting to inventory levels, which underpin our profitability across our extensive store network as we tackle supply chain issues, softer non-essential demand, and omnichannel shifts. Total inventory ended Q2 at $1.18 billion, down 14.2% from $1.38 billion in Q2 2023—third straight quarter of declines, lowest since pre-pandemic Q4 2021. Comp-store basis, excluding 45 net new units, it's 16.1% lower, fueling 210 basis points of gross margin to 38.4% via fewer markdowns.

By category: apparel/softlines (32% mix) down 22% to $378 million after 18% SKU cuts, emphasizing bestsellers like private-label activewear turning 6.2x versus Target's 5.8x. Footwear/accessories down 19% to $212 million on strong sell-through. Home goods/decor (elevated from housing slowdowns) fell 12% to $285 million, electronics/durables down 8% to $331 million for back-to-school builds, grocery/essentials minimally down 5% to $260 million for EDLP.

U.S. (85% total) dropped 15.8%, Southeast strongest at 19% amid tourism. Canada 12% decline despite currency, Europe pilot 21% to $95 million via DC tweaks.

Tech drives this: AI demand sensing on Manhattan WMS/Snowflake hits 92% accuracy, cutting stockouts 27%. RFID on 65% U.S. hardlines reduces shrink to 1.2%, enables real-time counts in 1,200 stores. JIT with P&G/Stanley cuts lead times to 28 days, cross-docking 40% inbound. Q3 OTB $850 million, 11% below last year.

Turns at 5.1x TTM versus 4.3x YoY and 4.8x sector median, DIO 72 days from 85. Q3 down another 8-10% YoY, boosting FCF over 95% of EBITDA while balancing BOPIS at 18% sales.

Next, our omnichannel initiatives progress, central to blending digital and physical for seamless experiences amid 2.8% Q2 comps and discretionary softness. Omnichannel sales—digital orders via 1,200+ stores—hit $1.2 billion, up 28% YoY, 42% of e-comm GMV from 32%, ahead of 40% target and matching Target's 35%. BOPIS $785 million (65%), up 32% on 15% app growth, AOV $85 (12% above pure digital) with bundles. Curbside up 18% to 420,000 orders under 8 minutes, lifting store conversions 22%, 40% add-on buys like Walmart's. Added 150 bps to margins via 45% shipping savings.

RetailFlow microservices with Manhattan/Oracle gives 98% real-time visibility, BOPIS out-of-stocks 2.1% from 5.8%. Geofencing 1.2 million promos up attach 8%, Google Vertex AI pilot 14% pick accuracy in 200 stores scaling Q1. $45 million YTD at 3.5x ROI.

Sunbelt at 52% penetration, 41% BOPIS growth on traffic/demand. Midwest/Northeast 22% via store-hub, Chicago radii cut 60%. Omnichannel LTV 2.7x higher, NPS 68 from 54, retention 82%, +3.2 comp points.

Priorities: same-day ship-from-store 80% SKUs by year-end (30% AOV pilots), kiosks 400 stores for returns/AR (25% repurchase), 2x loyalty points for 55% penetration FY26. Core to 5-7% comp algorithm, holiday BOPIS +35% QoQ.

We are maintaining a strong balance sheet and are well positioned to invest in our growth initiatives.

Before questions, let me outline the key assumptions under our affirmed full-year fiscal 2024 guidance: revenue growth 4% to 6% or $28.5 billion to $29.2 billion; comp store sales 2% to 4%; adjusted operating income $2.1 billion to $2.3 billion with 20-50 bps margin expansion; diluted EPS $8.50 to $9.20. Physical stores at 72% sales anchor our omnichannel approach.

Macro: PCE inflation 2.5-2.7%, CPI to 2.8%, rates 4.75-5.00%, 2-3% disposable income growth for $50K-$100K demo. Industry comps +1.5%, our home essentials/apparel +3%/+2.5%, BOPIS 150 bps aid.

Consumers value-focused, 68% loyalty to private label/promos to 32% sales, 100 bps margin via Vietnam/Mexico. Staples +5%, H&B +4% GLP-1. Traffic +1-2% via Store of Future (40% conversion), e-comm 28% sales, MFCs 200 bps fulfillment.

Margins: gross +40-60 bps to 28.5% from $120M freight, shrink 1.3% (-20 bps) RFID 80% apparel/600 stores, promos 12% sales. SG&A -75 bps to 20.8% occupancy/labor AI (FourKites/Workforce.com), headcount flat 180,000, wages +3.5%.

Capex $650M: 25 new Sunbelt stores, 150 remodels curbside +30% BOPIS, $150M two automated DCs Texas/Ohio 1M cases/week. Turns 5.2x, weeks supply 12.

Sunbelt +6-8% comps migration/traffic, Northeast flat-+1% wallet share. Canada/Mexico +3%, nearshoring.

Brick tactile edge home +400 bps comps, Rewards 55M members +2 visits (42% opens), 50% recycled packaging Gen Z.

Risks: high rates home (-EPS minimal), tariffs 50 bps COGS stress-tested. Upside traffic/margins. 100 bps comp miss $200M top-line, 45% EBITDA buffer.

Balanced, precise execution for the range.

Now, let's open the line for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. [Operator Instructions] Our first question comes from Alex Rivera with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera (Goldman Sachs):
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the impact of moderating inflation on your sales?

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Good morning, Alex. Inflation easing to around 2.8% CPI has been supportive, particularly for our middle-income core where disposable income grew 2-3%. We've seen consumers shift to value plays like our private label up 12% comps, offsetting any discretionary softness—essentials and health/beauty outperformed at +5% and +4%. Our omnichannel BOPIS helped capture this, adding 150 bps to comps without heavy discounting. Overall, it positions us well for sustained traffic.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Jordan Lee with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Jordan Lee (JPMorgan):
What are your expectations for same-store sales growth in the next quarter?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Thanks, Jordan. For Q3, we expect comp store sales growth of 4% to 6%, incorporating 1-2% traffic uplift from Store of the Future experiential zones and 18% BOPIS momentum, plus category strength in staples. This assumes moderating inflation and no major consumer pullback, with Sunbelt leading at 6-8%. We're conservative on Northeast but see omnichannel lifting overall.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Taylor Kim with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Taylor Kim (Morgan Stanley):
Thanks. On inventory, how are you thinking about holiday builds given the YoY declines?

Lisa Chen, Chief Financial Officer:
Great question, Taylor. We're entering Q3 with tight OTB at $850 million, 11% below prior, focused on high-velocity holiday SKUs. Expect another 8-10% YoY decline overall, but strategic builds in electronics and seasonal for back-to-school/holiday. Turns stay elevated at 5.2x full-year via AI forecasting and RFID, balancing BOPIS needs—avoiding Macy's stockout issues while driving FCF.

Operator:
Thank you. That concludes today's questions.

Mike Thompson, Chief Executive Officer:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, we are pleased with our progress this quarter and remain focused on executing our long-term strategy. Thank you for your continued support.

Sarah Johnson, Head of Investor Relations:
This concludes today's call. Thank you for joining us.
